current_episode.title: FORUM FOCUS PODCAST: NECA's Doug Martin on 45 Years of Management-Labor Collaboration

guest.entreprise: St. Louis Chapter National Electrical Contractors Association (NECA)
guest.bio_context: Doug Martin grew up in western Montana in a copper mining family, with his grandfather holding multiple leadership positions including president in Local One of the Miners Union in Butte, which had over 40,000 members at its peak. After college, he worked as an explosive apprentice in the mines for less than two years before being encouraged to leave the industry. He joined NECA as a trainee in fall 1977 through the association's national office recruiting program, became assistant manager in March 1978, and has spent over 40 years building labor-management collaboration in the St. Louis construction industry.

context.real_quote: I've worked my whole career with an organization that simply wanted to build an appropriate and productive relationship with our labor partners.

We are the proud sponsor, Forum Focus, because when we dream big, we all rise together. Welcome to Forum Focus, the podcast, Construction Forum. I'm Tom Finan, the Executive Director and Co-Founder of the Forum. On Forum Focus, you'll hear the stories of stakeholders in the St. Louis region's built environment. They're working to create inclusive, robust employment and economic growth. Forum Focus is diverse, it's unbiased, and it's civil. I first met Doug Martin almost 45 years ago. Doug recently stepped down as Executive Director of the St. Louis Chapter National Electrical Contractors Association, known as NECA. He now serves as co-chair of the St. Louis Construction Cooperative. It didn't take long after we met for me to become friends with this descendant of a Butte, Montana, copper mining family. We bonded over a shared passion for the people of another family, the St. Louis construction industry. After college, Doug thought he would wind up representing union miners in labor affairs. But the demise of the mining industry and another series of events landed him in St. Louis at NECA. That occurred just as my career as a publisher in the construction industry was starting. Over the years, Doug has demonstrated his dedication to the industry, not only by relentless work ethic, but by a steadfast, and some would say stubborn, focus on issues such as diversity, worker welfare, and economic growth. He is respected for his ability to build lasting relationships. Doug knows his facts, and he sticks to his guns, whether that's in labor negotiations or lobbying legislators to defeat right to work. When asked to describe my relationship with Doug, I always say, he's someone I would trust to have my back in a knife fight. Please listen to this podcast with Doug Martin. So we've known one another for a while. We have. I don't remember exactly when we met, but you were one of the very first people I worked with in St. Louis when I started working for the chapter. I want to say the first time you and I met was when Vern introduced us working on a project in 1978. I started with a chapter, came in as a special project, as a trainee out of the national office in the fall of 77. The chapter staff at that point had a couple of people out for healthy reasons, and I ended up basically not leaving, even though I was supposed to be traveling the whole region at that point. and then the chapter offered me a job as an assistant manager in March of 1978. How did you wind up with NECA in the first place in Washington? Long story of basically being out of work. I grew up, as you know, in western Montana. My family were all in the area around Montana. Many of them worked around the mines in the mining industry. When I went to college, I took labor relations as part of my business curriculum, really thinking that I would try to go to work for the miners' union on the labor side of the equation. By the time I graduated from college, the Panaconda Company, which was basically the sole provider of jobs for that region, decided to close down U.S. operations. I did go to work in the mines for a little less than two years. I was actually an explosive apprentice, as well as you know me. You can picture that. It was a destiny for failure. But not only did I hate it, but my granddad, who was still involved with the minor junior, realized I was not going to have a successful career underground. And he kind of encouraged me in a very less diplomatic way to get out. And is that recall he blew up your lunchbox? Well, he didn't. But my journeyman that I was working for just started letting me know that he thought I was worthless and that, you know, I should get out while the getting was good. And he liked to play games with blasting caps. And on one particular day, he did blow up my lunchbox. That's sort of a message that I really wasn't welcome on his crew.

pending_qa.q: What community impact did joint labor-management electrical work achieve in St. Louis?
pending_qa.r: The collaborative effort between NECA contractors and IBEW union electricians produced tangible civic contributions, including electrical and communication work on nearly all Habitat for Humanity homes in the St. Louis region, with only a handful of homes in the entire region where joint contribution did not occur. The partnership also relit the St. Louis Science Center planetarium after years of darkness, creating what Doug Martin describes as a lasting sense of civic pride that represents how good businesses and labor leaders working together achieve better results.
